Rafael Tobias 56.7% / Lucas Fernando 43.3%, with a wide engine split (GBM 55.7%, hand-tuned 36.6%) and both fighters carrying a computed trust of 0.214 — the lowest figures on the card by a wide margin. Each man has exactly one UFC fight and 15.0 minutes of divisional data, and each lost it.

At that trust level both composite sets are shrunk almost all the way to the light-heavyweight mean, and they come out nearly indistinguishable: power -0.15 against -0.16, chin +0.16 against +0.17, output -0.42 against -0.39, cardio +0.20 against +0.25. The only real separations are reach, where Fernando leads +1.58 to -0.67 (203.2cm to 187.96cm), and strength of schedule, where Tobias reads 0.856 against Fernando's 1.222. The 13.5-point margin is essentially the model's read on Tobias being 23.4 years old to 29.6 and considerably more recently active.

The consequence is the flattest fight shape on the card. The decision rate is 69.3% — the highest of the twelve — and the finish rate only 30.7%, because neither man has a UFC finish and both read 0.000 on finishing ability. That makes this the longest projected fight on the card, with the Over 1.5 at 80.3% and the Over 2.5 at 73.6%. Two further caveats belong on the record: Fernando has never fought at light heavyweight in the UFC (his single bout was at middleweight) and arrives on a 1,097-day layoff — just over three years — so what the model is actually reading is a 13-3 pre-UFC record of sixteen fights wearing a divisional prior. Whatever the number says, this is a coin flip.

matchupAnalysis: The narrowest projection on the card: Vicente Luque 56.3% / Tresean Gore 43.7%, with the hand-tuned model more confident (64.1%) than the GBM (53.2%). What makes it interesting is the mismatch between the decision edge and the win probability. Luque's decision edge is +2.115, the second-widest on the card, and his Elo advantage is decisive at 1885 across twenty-five divisional fights to 1576 across seven — and he still only projects at 56%. Luque is also moving up: twenty-four of his twenty-five UFC fights were at welterweight, though his most recent, a first-round submission of Kelvin Gastelum, was at middleweight.

The reason the decision edge does not translate is that only 34.9% of sims reach the judges. This is the most finish-heavy fight on the card at 65.1%, with 36.6% of all sims ending in round one. On any round-winning basis Gore is badly beaten: his output composite reads -2.93, the most extreme single value anywhere on this card, with chin -1.61 and power -0.84. Luque's +0.60 power against that chin produces a 26.6% knockout, the modal terminal state.

But Gore's 43.7% is almost entirely one number, and it is the largest single method share belonging to any fighter on this card: a 29.5% submission. His raw submission finish rate is 1.000 — every career finish he owns is a submission, including a round-three finish of Azamat Bekoev in April and a round-one finish of Antonio Trocoli — and his wrestling defense (+0.91) is the best figure in the fight. Luque is a live target for it: chin -0.61, chin-damage factor 0.753, a 0.375 career finished-rate, and two submission losses in recent memory including Kevin Holland in round two. Luque's October decision loss was to Joel Alvarez, who fights earlier on this card.

Low confidence — and the reason is Gore's 29.5% submission, the largest single method share of any fighter on this card, off a 1.000 raw submission finish rate against a Luque who reads -0.61 chin, 0.375 finished-rate and has two recent submission losses. Luque's +2.115 decision edge is the second-widest here and barely matters, because only 34.9% of sims reach the judges.

His +2.764 submission-threat index is the largest on the card and converts to a 27.8% submission, his best single route, with a 15.9% knockout and a 40.1% decision behind it.

The problem is everything around it. He is 39.8 years old to Orolbai's 28.5, with an age factor of 0.805, a 281-day layoff and a recent-three win rate of 0.333 against Orolbai's 1.000, who has won three straight including a first-round knockout of Jack Hermansson. Reasonably high confidence: near-full trust on both sides, a -212 Elo gap, and an 11.3-year age difference running the right way. Wells is the better striker on the measured rates (+1.065 strike differential, card-best 0.700 head strikes absorbed per minute) but is 39.8 years old off a 281-day layoff.
